planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Doerfler's thyme forms a dense, low, silvery mat prized as much for its felted foliage as for its flowers.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Doerfler's thyme forms a dense, mat-forming carpet of small, gray-green, softly hairy leaves that give the foliage a silvery, felted appearance distinct from smoother-leaved culinary thymes. Clusters of small, rich pink to rose-lilac flowers cover the mat in late spring to early summer, drawing bees heavily and creating a striking two-toned effect against the silvery foliage. Like other creeping thymes, it tolerates light foot traffic and is well suited to planting between stepping stones, along path edges, or cascading over a low rock wall, releasing a mild aromatic scent when brushed or stepped on. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which shortens its life.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun, ideally at the top of a wall or in a hanging container; Lebanese oregano is grown almost entirely for its cascading habit and ornamental flowers rather than for culinary use.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun, ideally where its trailing stems can cascade over the edge of a raised bed, wall, or hanging basket; Lebanese oregano is grown chiefly as an ornamental rather than a culinary herb, producing long, wiry stems draped with rounded, blue-green leaves and dangling clusters of papery, chartreuse-pink, hop-like bracts that persist attractively for weeks in mid- to late summer. The trailing habit and long-lasting bracted flower clusters make it a favorite for dry, sunny container plantings and rock wall crevices where its cascade can be fully appreciated. It is somewhat more tender than common culinary oregano, so provide winter protection or grow it as a container plant that can be moved to shelter in climates colder than its hardiness range. Trim lightly after the main flowering display fades to keep growth tidy, and avoid rich soil or excess water, both of which produce leggy, less floriferous growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yerba buena is a California and Pacific Northwest woodland native that spreads as a low, trailing groundcover under trees.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yerba buena is a trailing California and Pacific Coast native mint relative that forms a loose, low groundcover of small, rounded, glossy leaves with a refreshing, minty fragrance released when brushed or crushed. Historically brewed as a mild, pleasant herbal tea by Native Californians and early Spanish settlers (the plant lent its name to the original Spanish name for the settlement that became San Francisco), it remains valued today mostly as a fragrant, shade-tolerant groundcover rather than a major culinary herb. Small, inconspicuous white to pale lavender flowers appear in the leaf axils in summer, largely incidental to the plant's soft-textured foliage display. It spreads gently by trailing, rooting stems under open tree canopy, tolerating dry shade better than many groundcovers once established, making it a good low-maintenance choice for woodland garden paths and understory plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; Sonoma sage spreads by rooting stems to form a low, wide-spreading groundcover mat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; Sonoma sage is a low, mat-forming California native groundcover with soft, gray-green, aromatic leaves and short spikes of pale lavender-blue flowers held just above the foliage in late spring, drawing bees and occasional hummingbirds. Trailing stems root as they spread, gradually covering considerable ground and making it a valuable low-water groundcover alternative to turf on dry slopes, under oaks, and in chaparral-style landscaping. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established, going dormant or semi-dormant with reduced leaf size during the hottest, driest part of summer and flushing fresh growth with fall and winter rains, in keeping with its Mediterranean-climate origins. Avoid summer irrigation on established plantings, which encourages root rot and fungal problems in this drought-adapted native.
